title: Your Fear of AI Is About the Size of Your Plans
summary: When AI makes building cheap, small plans feel threatened and big ones get fuel. Why to aim bigger, what Jevons really found, and what the hiring data warns.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
A teammate demos a coding agent at the Friday sync. In about ten minutes it scaffolds the admin screen your team had estimated at a full sprint. Two people watch the same demo. One thinks, "Well, there goes my sprint." The other thinks, "Great, so we can finally build the offline mode we've pushed back for two years."

Same tool, same ten minutes, opposite feelings. Garry Tan named the difference in a February 2026 essay: "Our fear of the future is directly proportional to how small our ambitions are" (Boil the ocean). I think he's mostly right. This post is an engineer's read of his argument: the part that holds up, what the old economics behind it actually says, and the job data that should keep all of us honest.

The zero-sum reading

The first reaction to a strong AI demo is usually some fast math. It does what I do, it costs less, so where does that leave me? That math assumes a fixed pie. If the tool takes a slice, there's less left for you.

Lots of teams then play exactly that game. They use AI to close the same backlog a bit faster, shave a few percent off the budget and call it a strategy. Nothing wrong with saving money. It's also the smallest possible use of the tool, and it puts you in a race against software on the one axis where software always wins: doing a known task again, for less.

Fear scales with the plan

Tan's line works as a test you can run on yourself. If the whole plan is to keep doing exactly what you do today, a tool that does it faster really is a threat. If the plan includes things you couldn't have attempted before, the same tool is the best news you've had in years.

That doesn't make the fear silly. Some people have solid reasons to worry, and the numbers are further down. It does mean the first question to ask is about your plan, and only then about the tool.

Goals that stopped being slogans

Every team keeps a list of things everyone agrees would be great and nobody will ever fund: read every support ticket, test every edge case, keep the docs in sync with the code. They come up in planning, everyone nods, and they're gone by the next sprint.

When drafting code, tests and docs gets this cheap, a good part of that list turns into ordinary engineering work. Tan's own example is talking to every single user and understanding every bug in the product. Here's the same team and budget with a small plan and with a bigger one:

Same budget, small planSame budget, bigger plan
Skim a sample of support tickets once a sprint.Have every ticket read, tagged and linked to a bug or a feature request each week.
Test the happy path plus the edge cases someone remembers.Generate property-based tests across the input space and review the ones that fail.
Document the five endpoints people ask about most.Document every endpoint and update the docs in the same PR as the code.
Trim cost a few percent on the product you already have.Ask what would make users happily pay far more, then go find the path.

The right column still needs people. Someone decides which tickets matter, reviews the generated tests and owns the release. What changed is that typing stopped being the bottleneck, so the size of the plan became the limit.

From doing tasks to building things

What you do with this depends on where you sit. The direction is the same for everyone: up.

  • If you're an individual contributor, pick something you'd never have tried alone. The internal tool your team keeps asking for, the side project you shelved, the migration nobody wants to write. One person with good AI tools can now cover design, code, docs and tests at a level that used to need a small team. You still own the result, bugs included.
  • If you lead a team or hold a budget, watch out for the easy win. Cutting people to nudge the margin is the smallest bet on the table. The better question is what you could build that customers would gladly pay much more for, and which of your people already know that product best.
Swap the question

Stop asking "how do I do my current job a little cheaper?" Ask "what could my team build this quarter that we never dared to put on the roadmap?" The first question makes the tool your competitor. The second makes it a teammate.

Why cheaper work tends to mean more work

The fear assumes that more automation means less work overall. Two old ideas push the other way, and both are worth knowing from the original.

In 1938, in Nine Chains to the Moon, Buckminster Fuller described "ephemeralization": doing more and more with less and less (about the book). He meant it as good news, a civilization getting more out of every unit of material and effort.

About seventy years earlier, William Stanley Jevons studied coal. "It is wholly a confusion of ideas to suppose that the economical use of fuel is equivalent to a diminished consumption. The very contrary is the truth," he wrote in The Coal Question (chapter VII). His evidence: in Scotland, iron makers cut the coal needed per ton of iron to less than a third, and total coal use went up about tenfold, because cheap iron found uses nobody had bothered with before. Economists now call this the Jevons paradox.

More efficient ≠ less work

Apply Jevons to software and the bet goes like this: make building cheap, and people will want software in places nobody could afford it before. It's a reasonable bet. It's still a bet, and the next section is about what it needs.

Now the part optimistic essays tend to skip. Jevons talks about total demand. He says nothing about who gets hired first. Stanford's Digital Economy Lab tracks this with ADP payroll data covering millions of US workers. In the August 2026 revision of their paper, the authors found no sign of economy-wide job loss from AI. They did find that employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations was 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, while experienced workers showed no such gap. The drop came mostly from fewer hires, and it sat in jobs where AI substitutes for the work. Where AI complements people, employment was flat or rising. The authors call these early, descriptive signals and say clearly that they aren't causal estimates (Canaries in the Coal Mine?, checked November 2026).

It doesn't switch on by itself

Tan makes a related point: the Jevons effect doesn't activate on its own. It needs people with budgets and authority to raise their ambitions. If everyone uses AI to do the same small thing a bit cheaper, demand doesn't grow, and the savings just mean fewer people doing the same work.

The Stanford split also gives a practical hint, for people early in their career and for whoever hires them. Hiring shrank where AI replaces the task. It held up where AI helps a person do more. So aim your learning at the second kind of work: own a feature end to end, get good at reviewing and testing what the model writes, sit closer to users. And if you lead a team, keep hiring juniors and hand them real scope. A bigger plan needs more people who understand the product, and today's juniors are where those people come from.

Good startups have always worked this way. In Tan's words, they build "for the 10x future while everyone else is optimizing for the 1.05x present." You don't need to found a startup to borrow the habit. You need one goal that's clearly bigger than last quarter's, and a plan for who on the team grows into it.

Try this week

  • Write down one thing your team has called "too expensive" for more than a year. Estimate it again, assuming AI drafts the code, tests and docs.
  • List the tasks you do every week. Mark which ones AI could replace and which ones it helps you do more of. Move a few hours toward the second group.
  • If you lead a team, put one goal on next quarter's roadmap that you'd have laughed at two years ago.
  • If you mentor a junior, give them a slice of that goal they can own from start to finish.

That Friday demo will keep coming back, a bit better every month. How it feels depends mostly on the size of the plan you bring to it. For a closer look at how the jobs themselves are shifting, read how AI changes software roles.

faqs.q: Why does AI scare some people and excite others?
faqs.a: It usually comes down to the plan. If your plan is to keep doing exactly what you do today, a tool that does it faster and cheaper is a real threat. If your plan includes work you could never afford before, the same tool is fuel. Garry Tan put it as "Our fear of the future is directly proportional to how small our ambitions are" in his February 2026 essay Boil the ocean.

In The Coal Question (1865), William Stanley Jevons argued that using fuel more efficiently tends to increase total fuel use. His example: Scottish iron makers cut coal per ton of iron to under a third, and total coal use rose about tenfold because cheap iron found many new uses. Applied to AI, the bet is that cheaper software work will create demand for much more software.

faqs.q: Will AI create more jobs or fewer?
faqs.a: Nobody knows yet, and the early data is mixed. Stanford's Digital Economy Lab (August 2026 revision, ADP payroll data) found no economy-wide job loss from AI. It also found that employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations was 19% below where it would have been had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, mostly through fewer hires. Experienced workers showed no such gap. The authors call these early signals, not causal proof.

faqs.q: I'm early in my career. What should I focus on?
faqs.a: Aim for work where AI helps you do more, since that is where the Stanford data shows employment holding up. Own features end to end, get good at reviewing and testing AI-written code, and stay close to users and the product. Use AI to take on bigger scope sooner, and keep the judgment calls as your own.
